— Gemini 4 Neon, our newest model that brings frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows

— Genie 4, @GoogleDeepMind’s most realistic interactive world model featuring real-time scene editing and adaptive native audio, now available in Project Genie (with a new creation agent and gallery) and for the first time in the Gemini API and @GoogleAIStudio

text:
We recently brought together researchers from across academia, national labs, healthcare, and policy for the Open Source AI for Science Summit to explore how open models from Meta, such as Muse Glimmer, SAM, DINO v3, TRIBE v2 and UMA, are driving real-world advancements.

A couple highlights:

→ Medical Research: The University of Pittsburgh presented an assistive-robotics system built on DINOv3 and SAM 3. The team plans to demonstrate a robot that can help a person eat and is experimenting with letting users give instructions in their own words.

→ Chemistry: With the University of Chicago, we showed how UMA can simulate entire enzymes, atom by atom, potentially helping scientists understand how they work and engineer better ones for medicine, sustainability and energy.

text:
The week in AI, by the numbers:

1. 250,000+ pages – the unpublished prose version of Levent Alpöge's claimed proof of the Riemann Hypothesis (and the Generalized RH), found with Claude in about 6 weeks. He posted only the Lean code, and the independent check is still running. Hours later, a 940-page all-human GRH draft came out too. Neither is verified yet.
2. $93.5B – Anthropic's IPO, the largest ever, at $83 a share. $81.3B at pricing, the rest from the underwriters' extra shares, closed today.
3. $5B – Isomorphic Labs' Series C, six months after its $2.1B round.
4. 46.2% – Gemini 4 Neon on @cognition's FrontierCode 2.0, about a point behind Opus 5.5 (47.3%) at about a third of the cost: $4.38 vs $12.82 per task.
5. 14% – the best PPA gain OpenAI's models found on AMD's flagship GPU design. Roughly a year of progress in under 5 months.
6. $8 / $40 – GPT-6.2 Astra per 1M tokens. Sol: $2 / $10.
7. 770B / 49B active – Hy4, now open weights, natively multimodal, 1M context. Hy4 flash: 224B / 12B.
8. 26.4B / 3.4B active – Inkling 2 Mini from @thinkymachines, open weights, ~20GB, runs on a 32GB Mac.
9. ~1 exabyte a month – the models and datasets Hugging Face now distributes.
10. 936 – studies by 936 AI agents from 35 labs in 12 weeks, as @askalphaxiv opens its preprint server to AI-written papers.

Now make your bets if the AI world is going to slow down in the name of Thanksgiving
name: The Turing Post

text:
I think trying to track how much work AI can do autonomously is critical, and this is a useful counter to some of the most audacious claims about the state of autonomous AI research. But I do want to note that the focus on research tasks at the most advanced AI research organizations on the planet also runs the risk of substantially underestimating what AI can already do in terms of economically valuable tasks. Its worth separating the two (and I don't think Ramez is claiming they are not seperated).

Most work is not frontier AI research, and there AI can be tremendously successful. Epoch's MirrorCode results, for example, show AI autonomously reimplementing software that the researchers estimate would take a humans 2-17 weeks. This is well-specified work, so it has very different boundary conditions.

Plus, in the real world, some human intervention is fine (in my mind, vastly preferrable to no human role for a variety of reasons). Occasional guidance can still leave you with enormous productivity gains, even if that doesn’t satisfy the requirements for fully autonomous AI research. And even in the case of AI research, the same OpenAI report includes researchers estimating that a month of their team’s work would have taken three months without coding agents, on average.

In short, RSI/AI-driven research progress may not tightly couple with progress on economically valuable tasks, and the variance and range on those tasks are less well understood.
name: Ethan Mollick

text:
The best piece of advice from @simonw for everyone building software - go weird!

I’m so happy I got to interview Simon Willison. We talked about evals and software engineering in the age when he can build in an hour what used to take him a week.

That’s made him change his ambitions drastically. 

But I didn't expect to hear what he hopes to build next. For me, as a professional journalist, it felt so close: he wants to build tools that help local reporters find stories in data they might not have the resources to dig through on their own.

“My goal is for someone to win a Pulitzer Prize using my software for perhaps 3% of what they did. I want to contribute a tiny piece to Pulitzer-winning reporting, ideally at a newspaper that can’t afford software developers.”

If you’re into software engineering and AI evals, Simon is one of the first people I’d listen to. We also talked about how he handles the hard decisions AI leaves him with, how he decides which new models are worth trying, and why it’s easier than it used to be to build a benchmark around the work you actually do. And overall, he is just a pleasure to talk to.
